lessons.title: Meet Your Two Minds
lessons.key_idea: Your thinking runs on a fast, intuitive System 1 and a slow, effortful System 2, and the lazy System 2 often accepts System 1's quick answers without checking them.

lessons.title: What You See Is All There Is
lessons.key_idea: System 1 builds a confident story from whatever information is in front of it and ignores what is missing, so we jump to conclusions from too little evidence.

lessons.title: The Pull of Random Numbers
lessons.key_idea: Anchoring means any number we see first, even an obviously irrelevant one, drags our later estimates toward it.

lessons.title: Why We Trust Our Gut Too Much
lessons.key_idea: We are overconfident because a coherent story feels true, which makes us overrate our predictions and underestimate how long plans will take.

lessons.title: Losses Hurt More Than Gains
lessons.key_idea: Prospect theory shows that we judge outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point, and a loss feels roughly twice as painful as an equal gain feels good.

lessons.title: The Experiencing and Remembering Selves
lessons.key_idea: We remember experiences by their peak moment and their ending, not their total duration, so the self that makes choices is guided by memories that distort what we actually lived through.

lessons.title: Catching Your Mind in the Act
lessons.key_idea: We can't switch off System 1, but we can learn to recognize situations where errors are likely and deliberately slow down when the stakes are high.

plan.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
plan.author: Daniel Kahneman
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's structure, core concepts and best-known examples in detail, though I may not recall every minor study precisely.
plan.one_liner: Your mind runs on two systems, and the fast one is quietly making most of your decisions.
plan.summary: Nobel-winning psychologist Daniel Kahneman explains how our thinking is shaped by two modes. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive. System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful, and also rather lazy. Most of the time System 1 serves us well, but it relies on mental shortcuts that lead to predictable errors. Drawing on decades of research, much of it with his collaborator Amos Tversky, Kahneman shows how we jump to conclusions from limited information, get pulled by irrelevant numbers, trust our judgments more than we should, and fear losses far more than we value equal gains. He also reveals a split between how we experience life and how we remember it. The book doesn't promise to fix our minds. It gives us a vocabulary to recognize when our intuitions are likely to mislead us.
